questions.q: Name the 1878 international conference that revised the Treaty of San Stefano and recognized the independence of Serbia, Montenegro, and Romania while placing Bosnia-Herzegovina under Austro-Hungarian administration.
questions.a: The Congress of Berlin (1878). A wrong answer (e.g., Congress of Vienna 1815 or Treaty of Versailles 1919) reveals confusion about the timeline of great power diplomacy in the Balkans and the specific settlement that set up the 1908 annexation crisis.

questions.q: Explain why the Bosnian Crisis of 1908–09 damaged relations between Austria-Hungary and Serbia, and why Russia backed down despite supporting Serbia.
questions.a: Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina (formally Ottoman but under Austro-Hungarian administration since 1878), infuriating Serbia which wanted those territories for a South Slav kingdom. Russia backed down because it was militarily unprepared after the 1905 Russo-Japanese War and needed German support elsewhere. A wrong answer that says "Russia didn't care" or "Serbia accepted it" shows misunderstanding of the prestige and alliance dynamics that made the crisis a rehearsal for 1914.

questions.q: A 1912 map shows the Balkan League (Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece, Montenegro) attacking the Ottoman Empire. Using the concept of "nationalism as a unifying and dividing force," explain why the League formed and why it collapsed into the Second Balkan War (1913) within months.
questions.a: The League united on the nationalist goal of expelling the Ottomans from Europe (unifying force). It collapsed because the victors quarreled over partitioning Macedonia — Bulgaria attacked its former allies Serbia and Greece, leading to the Second Balkan War where Bulgaria lost territory (dividing force). A wrong answer that only mentions "they fought over land" misses the nationalist logic: each state claimed the same territories based on ethnic populations, showing how nationalism creates overlapping, irreconcilable claims.

questions.q: Compare the role of great powers in the 1878 Congress of Berlin and the 1912–13 Balkan Wars. How did the shift from "concert of Europe" management to "local initiative" increase the risk of general war?
questions.a: In 1878, Bismarck chaired a congress where great powers imposed a settlement to maintain balance. In 1912–13, the Balkan League acted independently, fighting the Ottomans and each other while great powers (especially Austria-Hungary and Russia) could only react, not control. This shift meant local nationalist wars could escalate without great power consent — exactly what happened in 1914 when Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia triggered the alliance system. A wrong answer that says "great powers always controlled events" ignores the critical loss of diplomatic control after 1908.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo (1914) was the inevitable result of Balkan nationalism alone." Use evidence from the 1878–1913 period to support your judgment.
questions.a: The claim is partially true but incomplete. Balkan nationalism provided the motive (Young Bosnia wanted South Slav unity), but the assassination became a world-historical trigger because: 1) Austria-Hungary used it as a pretext to crush Serbia (great power calculation), 2) The alliance system (Triple Alliance vs. Triple Entente) turned a bilateral crisis continental. Without the 1908 annexation creating the grievance, the 1912–13 wars emboldening Serbia, and the rigid alliances, the assassination might have remained a local crisis. A wrong answer that says "nationalism caused WWI directly" oversimplifies; one that says "nationalism was irrelevant" ignores the assassin's motives.

questions.q: Construct a timeline (1875–1914) with 6 key events showing the escalation of Balkan tensions. For each event, write one phrase identifying whether it was driven primarily by "ethnic nationalism," "Ottoman decline," or "great power rivalry."
questions.a: Sample timeline: 1875–78 Herzegovinian Uprising (ethnic nationalism/Ottoman decline); 1878 Congress of Berlin (great power rivalry); 1908 Bosnian Annexation Crisis (great power rivalry/ethnic nationalism); 1912 First Balkan War (ethnic nationalism); 1913 Second Balkan War (ethnic nationalism); 1914 Sarajevo Assassination (ethnic nationalism/great power rivalry). A poor answer lists events without categorizing drivers, or mislabels drivers (e.g., calling the Congress of Berlin "ethnic nationalism"), showing inability to distinguish the three causal strands.
